paper.authors_full: Zhihao Zhou, Letao Xiao, Jiayi Wang, Shuai Tong, Wenyu Zhang, Ning Hao
paper.title: Group-AI Collaboration Enhances Creativity Performance: The Roles of Perspective-Taking and AI Utilisation Strategies
paper.pdf_filename: Zhou et al (2026) - Group AI Collaboration Enhances Creativity Performance.pdf
paper.version_read: Undated blinded preprint marked as under double-blind journal review on PDF p. 1; PDF metadata is dated 2025-07-29. The supplied retrieval and citation records identify it as EdArXiv version 2, DOI 10.35542/osf.io/5a3mn_v2, posted 2025-08-04. It is not the later Journal of Computer Assisted Learning version of record.
paper.one_line_finding: Pairs in which each member had ChatGPT-4o produced ideas that two LLM judges rated more useful than human-only pairs (M = 4.09 vs 3.24; β = 0.84, SE = 0.04) and than people working alone with ChatGPT-4o (3.34; β = 0.74, SE = 0.06), and more original (3.68 vs 2.74 and 2.70; β = 0.94, SE = 0.05 and β = 0.98, SE = 0.07), while fluency did not differ and working alone with AI did not differ from human-only pairs (p > 0.05) (pp. 15-16, Section 3.1; p. 17, Figure 3).

studies.label: Within-subject laboratory experiment: scientific divergent application task
studies.cluster_se_treatment: Section 3.1 uses a Subject ID random effect. No separate team random effect or adjustment for dependence between teammates is reported. Pair-condition score aggregation, team counts, and allocation counts for condition-order sequences are not printed (PDF pp. 7-8, 11, 15-16).

counts_source.locator: PDF p. 7, Section 2.1 Participants; all participants completed every condition, PDF p. 8, Section 2.2
counts_source.quote: A total of 100 participants were recruited via an online questionnaire. Four participants were excluded for failing to follow task instructions, resulting in a final sample of 96

arms.name: Group-AI (G-AI)
arms.description: Two-person team shares a QQ Chat idea panel and takes turns contributing ideas. Each member has ChatGPT-4o and can ask a single task-related question during each of their own turns (PDF pp. 8-9, Section 2.2 and Figure 1 caption).

arms.name: Individual-AI (I-AI)
arms.description: Participant works one-on-one with ChatGPT-4o; the idea panel is private and shows only their own input (PDF pp. 8-9, Section 2.2 and Figure 1 caption).

arms.name: Human-only group (G)
arms.description: Two-person team takes turns contributing ideas in a shared QQ Chat panel; the AI interface is disabled. The human partner is the other aid (PDF pp. 8-9, Section 2.2 and Figure 1 caption).

studies.task: Generate novel applications for transparent ceramics, electronic skin, and crystal resin in scientific divergent application tasks, with material and condition order counterbalanced (PDF pp. 8, 10).

ai_tool.name: ChatGPT-4o (OpenAI)
ai_tool.locator: PDF p. 8, Section 2.2; the model release year is not stated

preregistration.where: No preregistration is stated in the saved manuscript; the power analysis in PDF p. 7, Section 2.1 is not a registration.

estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Ideas rated by ChatGPT-4o and DeepSeek on a five-point usefulness scale, from not at all useful to very useful. The paper does not state how idea scores or model ratings are aggregated for the condition means (PDF p. 10, Section 2.3).

regression.model: Mixed-effects model with collaboration condition as a fixed effect and Subject ID as a random effect (PDF p. 15, Section 3.1). No outcome standardization is described. Covariate inclusion and the covariance/SE estimator are not stated for these models.

estimates.notes: The three people counts refer to the same analyzed participants, each completing every condition (PDF pp. 7-8), and must not be added together. They are not independent observation counts. The paper does not print creativity-model observation counts or specify how pair-condition outputs and ratings were aggregated; unit, n_units, and sd_level are therefore null. No first-round-only results, paired-difference SDs, or within-person outcome correlations are reported. The paper calls these creativity outcomes primary (PDF p. 15), but no preregistration is stated. se_basis follows the stated Subject ID random effect under the extraction definition. This does not resolve whether shared team scores or residual dependence between partners were handled appropriately; pooling precision requires clarification. The printed SDs must not be assumed to be participant-level SDs. This contrast adds AI to the same human-pair setup. Outcome-specific participant inclusion and model sample sizes are not printed separately; the n fields identify the reported complete repeated-condition sample, not the number of independent rows underlying the means or standard errors.

Only a p-value bound is printed for this fixed-effect comparison; no coefficient, SE, or test statistic is supplied. se_basis follows the stated Subject ID random effect under the extraction definition. This does not resolve whether shared team scores or residual dependence between partners were handled appropriately; pooling precision requires clarification. The printed SDs must not be assumed to be participant-level SDs. The human partner is the active comparison aid. Construct fluency follows the number-of-ideas definition in codebook Section 6; the joint originality and usefulness threshold defines which ideas are counted and is retained in measure_detail. Higher values mean more high-quality ideas. Outcome-specific participant inclusion and model sample sizes are not printed separately; the n fields identify the reported complete repeated-condition sample, not the number of independent rows underlying the means or standard errors.

open_items: Creativity-score aggregation, the level of the printed SDs, and model observation counts are not stated. The Subject ID random effect does not establish how shared pair output and dependence between teammates were handled (PDF pp. 8, 10-11, 15-16). Do not treat the final people count as an independent outcome-row count.

The analyzed people count is reported for the experiment as a whole, with every participant completing every condition. Outcome-specific participant inclusion, analysis-row counts and model sample sizes are not printed separately; the retained people counts must not be treated as confirmed independent outcome counts (PDF pp. 7-8, 15-16).

No first-round-only creativity results, within-person correlations, or SDs of paired differences are printed. All extracted comparisons are from the repeated-condition results; the human-only condition is not separately reported by whether it preceded or followed AI (PDF pp. 7-8, 15-16).

Ordinary fluency has no printed condition means, SDs, test statistic, or p-value. Its qualitative no-difference result conflicts with the Discussion claim about increased idea volume (PDF pp. 16, 23).
The exact randomization/counterbalancing procedure and sequence counts are not stated. Section 2.2 and Figure 1B support random condition order but do not give its implementation (PDF pp. 7-9).
Counts at assignment, the precise exclusion stage, and the treatment of excluded participants’ partners are not printed. Only the final analyzed people count is used (PDF p. 7, Sections 2.1-2.2).

The covariates included in each creativity mixed-effects model and its covariance estimator are not specified. The paper lists pre-task control variables but does not state which entered Section 3.1 (PDF pp. 7, 10-11, 15-16).
The saved paper does not give ChatGPT-4o’s release year or a more specific model snapshot; ai_tool.year is null (PDF p. 8).
References to Supplementary Figure 2A and 2B may refer to the main-text classification figure. No separate supplement is supplied and no creativity statistic is said to be in it (PDF pp. 12, 14-15).
The later journal version has not been compared with this saved preprint. Post-review changes and internal discrepancies identified in the screening form remain unresolved.

The two high-quality perspective-taking rates are extracted as output-quality outcomes, but their analysis-specific people counts, observation counts, rate aggregation, SD levels, and handling of cases with no adopted ideas are not printed (PDF pp. 11-12, 17-18). The AI-rate comparison uses an independent-samples t-test despite the repeated-condition design; its reported d has no specified standardizer, and its negative t statistic differs in direction from the treatment-minus-control ordering of the means. These limitations remain unresolved; both estimates have se_basis unclear.
